title: Retries, TTL cache, and request dedupe for getUser
summary: getUser now shares one in-flight request between concurrent callers. fetchJson retries 429/502/503 with exponential backoff. Cache entries expire after 60s. Pay most attention to the failure paths: a rejected shared promise now fails every waiting caller at once, and retries multiply the latency of a failure.

nodes.label: In-flight dedupe in getUser
nodes.summary: Concurrent calls for the same id now share one promise.
nodes.explanation:
Before, two simultaneous `getUser(1)` calls both missed the cache and both hit the network. Now the first call stores its promise in `inflight`, and later callers return that same promise until it settles.

The `.finally` removes the entry on success **and** failure. A failed fetch is not cached, so the next call retries from scratch. Every caller that joined while the request was in flight sees the same rejection.

- The cache check changed from `if (hit)` to `hit !== undefined`, so falsy values like `0` or `""` are now real cache hits.
- The order matters. The cache is checked first, then `inflight`, then the fetch starts.

nodes.label: Retry with backoff in fetchJson
nodes.summary: 429, 502 and 503 are retried up to maxAttempts with exponential delay.
nodes.explanation:
Only statuses in `RETRYABLE` are retried. A 500 or 404 throws on the first attempt, as before.

The delay is `baseDelayMs * 2 ** (attempt - 1)`, so with defaults the waits are 200ms then 400ms. The third failure throws without waiting. A request that always returns 503 takes about 600ms plus three round trips to fail.

Network errors (fetch itself rejecting) are **not** caught. They still propagate immediately and are not retried.

nodes.label: 60s TTL on the cache
nodes.summary: Entries now store a timestamp and expire lazily on read.
nodes.explanation:
`set` stores `{ value, at }` instead of the raw value. `get` deletes and returns `undefined` when the entry is older than `TTL_MS`.

Expiry is lazy. Nothing sweeps the map, so keys that are never read again stay in memory forever. The optional `now` parameter exists so tests can control time without mocking `Date`.

nodes.label: Dedupe test
nodes.summary: Asserts two concurrent getUser calls make one fetch.
nodes.explanation:
The test mocks global `fetch` and checks the call count. It covers the happy path only. It does not exercise retries, rejection fan-out, or TTL expiry.

The module-level cache is shared across tests in the same file, so a later test asking for id `1` would get a cache hit.

questions.prompt: Three callers request user 7 at the same moment and the request returns 503 every time. What do they see?
choices: All three reject with the same error after the retries run out
The first rejects, the other two start fresh requests
Only the first caller retries; the others reject at once
questions.explanation: Callers two and three return the same promise from `inflight`, so the one rejection fans out to all of them. Nobody starts a second request while the first is pending.

questions.prompt: A request for user 7 fails. One second later someone calls getUser(7) again. What happens?
choices: A new fetch starts, because .finally removed the in-flight entry and errors are never cached
It returns the old rejected promise from inflight
questions.explanation: `.finally` runs on rejection too, deleting the `inflight` entry, and `cache.set` only runs in `.then`. So failures leave no trace and the next call fetches again.

questions.prompt: The API returns 0 for some user. Before this change, what did a second getUser call do?
choices: Fetched again, because `if (hit)` treated 0 as a miss
questions.explanation: The old check `if (hit)` is falsy for 0, so it refetched every time. The new `hit !== undefined` fixes that.

questions.prompt: With default options, the server returns 500 on every request. How many times is fetch called?
questions.explanation: 500 is not in `RETRYABLE` (only 429, 502, 503), so it throws on the first attempt.

questions.prompt: With defaults, the server returns 429 three times. How long does fetchJson spend sleeping before it throws?
questions.explanation: It sleeps after attempt 1 (200ms) and attempt 2 (400ms). Attempt 3 hits `attempt >= maxAttempts` and throws without sleeping, for 600ms in total.

questions.prompt: The DNS lookup fails and fetch() itself rejects. What does fetchJson do?
choices: Rejects immediately with the network error
questions.explanation: There is no try/catch around `await fetch(url)`. Only HTTP status codes are checked, so network errors propagate on the first attempt.

questions.prompt: A user is cached at t=0 and nobody asks for it again. What happens to that entry at t=5 minutes?
choices: It's still in the map. Expiry only happens when get() reads it
A timer deleted it at t=60s
It was evicted when the map grew
questions.explanation: Expiry is lazy. Only `get` checks the age and deletes. Unread keys stay in memory forever.

questions.prompt: Why do get and set take an optional `now` argument?
choices: So callers can backdate entries in production
So tests can control time without mocking Date
questions.explanation: Defaulting `now = Date.now()` keeps call sites unchanged while letting tests pass explicit timestamps.

questions.prompt: What does the store hold for a key after this change?
choices: { value, at } with the write timestamp
questions.explanation: `set` now stores `{ value, at: now }`, and `get` unwraps `.value`. Any other code reading the Map directly would now see the wrapper object.
